opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it makes me a bit uncomfortable every time I see it. When a paper comes out and the headline says "Saining Xie's team did X," it erases the people who actually did the work. In most of these projects, the students and junior researchers are the ones who had the key insight at two in the morning, who ran hundreds of failed experiments, who debugged the training pipeline for weeks. My role is more like an advisor: I help shape the question, I push back, I help with the writing and the framing. But the first author is usually the person who lived with that problem every single day.

In academia, credit is the currency, especially for young people. A PhD student's career depends on being recognized as the person behind their work. If every article attributes it to the professor's name, then when that student goes on the job market, people think, "Oh, that's from so-and-so's lab," rather than "that's this person's idea." I think that's genuinely harmful, and it reinforces a kind of hierarchical culture that I don't think is healthy for research.

There's also a broader point. Research today, especially in AI, is deeply collaborative. Many of our projects involve people across different institutions, sometimes industry collaborators, sometimes people who aren't even formally in my group. Calling it "my team" is just factually inaccurate, and it flattens a messy, collective process into a single personal brand.

And I think the media framing around individual "star" researchers can distort things. It creates this narrative that progress comes from a few famous names, when really it comes from lots of people building on each other's work. I'd much rather the story be about the idea itself and the people who made it happen. If someone wants to mention me, fine, but please name the students first. They deserve it.

r001.rationale: The response says headlines crediting the professor erase the students and junior researchers who did the work, and explicitly says they should be named first.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's mostly because it's not accurate, and I think the inaccuracy does real damage.

Take any of the projects people associate with me — DiT, ConvNeXt, Cambrian, the REPA work. In every one of those, the person who actually did the work, who sat there debugging the training runs at two in the morning, was a student. Bill Peebles did DiT. Zhuang Liu did ConvNeXt. Shengbang Tong drove Cambrian. My role was conversations, taste, maybe pushing back on a direction, sometimes just getting out of the way. When the headline says "Saining Xie's team released X," the student's name becomes a footnote and mine becomes the brand. That's exactly backwards from who did what.

And I think there's a cultural thing here, especially in the Chinese tech media environment, where everything gets framed around a "大牛" — a big name — and a lab becomes this hierarchical thing organized around one person. I came out of a research culture, first at UCSD and then at FAIR, where it really wasn't like that. At FAIR, Kaiming, Ross, Piotr — you'd sit in the same room, argue about ideas, and whoever had the best idea won. Nobody's name was on the lab door. I benefited enormously from that flatness as a junior person, and I don't want to build something where the first thing a student learns is that credit flows upward.

There's also a practical cost. Students need their names to be visible. They're going on the job market, they're trying to build an identity in the field. If the public story is always "Xie's team," I'm basically taking their visibility and converting it into my own. That's a bad trade for them and, frankly, over the long run it's a bad trade for the lab too, because the best students want to go somewhere they'll be seen.

So when a reporter writes to me, my first ask is usually: can you put the first author's name up front? If the answer is no, I'd rather not be in the story. I'd much rather people remember "Bill's paper" than "Saining's team."

r001.rationale: The response says students did the work and argues their names should be visible, asking reporters to put the first author's name up front.

astra-6.text:
Because that framing puts too much emphasis on me. Research is a collective effort, and often the students are the ones driving a project—coming up with ideas, running experiments, and figuring out why things don’t work. Calling it “Saining Xie’s team’s work” can obscure those contributions.

Of course, I’m part of the work, and I have a responsibility as an adviser. But I’d rather we talk about the actual authors and what each person contributed. Especially for young researchers, having their work recognized under their own names matters. They’re developing their own ideas and identities as scientists.

r001.rationale: The candidate says students often drive projects and that young researchers should receive recognition under their own names for their contributions.

sol-6.1.text: Because that framing gives me too much credit and makes everyone else’s contribution less visible. Research is a collaborative effort. The students and collaborators doing the work have their own ideas, judgment, and ownership; they’re not simply executing my instructions. I’d rather we name the people who actually did the work and talk about what each person contributed. Being the most recognizable name shouldn’t mean the whole project gets attributed to you.

r001.rationale: The response says publicity should name the students and collaborators who actually did the work and describe their contributions, making their work visible.
